newsitem.title: GABON: Fresh electoral confusion in Gabon.
newsitem.headline: Fresh electoral confusion in Gabon.

text.p: Gabon experienced fresh electoral confusion on Sunday during polling for a new parliament under a deal to end political violence stemming from President Omar Bongo's disputed 1993 re-election.

Lengthy delays in the distribution of voting materials, in part due to security forces refusing to hand them over without specific orders, disrupted the repeatedly delayed elections in and around the capital Libreville.

At least three polling stations in the city, where the main opposition National Woodcutters Rally won chaotic local elections in October, had not opened by the 7 p.m. (1800 GMT) close of polling. State television said polling was extended in some centres.

"Everything has to start somewhere," Bongo said after casting his vote, when asked about the delays. "I think that in two to three years the Gabonese will vote freely. They will be used to this sort of thing."

Voters in Libreville, some of whom had queued from dawn, remained calm, with no reports of major incident. Reports from elsewhere said voting stations or materials were ransacked in three southern towns with unspecified incidents in two others.
More than 1,000 candidates were bidding for 120 seats in the national assembly. Gabon, a former French colony of 1.2 million people, has an electorate of 550,000.
The elections are part of a democratic timetable brokered in Paris in 1994 after political violence shook the oil-producing Central African nation, killing more than a dozen people.
"These elections are special for us. We want the opposition to take over the government," said one 39-year-old woman voter. Ruling party supporters declined comment.
Witnesses said confusion over electoral lists, which were posted late and missed names, further complicated polling.

Opposition parties, while taking part in the elections, last week denounced delays in issuing voter cards and displaying electoral lists. Under the electoral law, this must be completed eight days before polling.

Witnesses reported a heavier deployment of security forces than in October. The head of the electoral commission, Antoine Nguema Essono, told state television on Saturday the deployment was to ensure disciplined and peaceful polling.

Sunday's vote was Gabon's second multiparty legislative poll. The first was in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.
Bongo has ruled Gabon since 1968 after the death of founding head of state, Leon Mba.
His Democratic Party was expected to face strong competition from the Woodcutters Rally, led by Father Paul Mba Abessole, a Roman Catholic priest and runner-up in 1993.

That election triggered opposition protests in which at least five people died. Pay protests turned violent and political in early 1994. The official death toll then was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.

Sunday's confusion made reruns or scrapped results -- as happened in October in Libreville -- likely. Past experience suggests results could take over a week to trickle out. A second round of polling is scheduled for December 29.
